value.overview: The Mountain Thrush (Turdus plebejus) is a highland thrush of Central America, associated mainly with cool, humid mountain forests. It is a resident species across most of its range, although individuals in Costa Rica move to lower elevations during the wettest part of the year. The species feeds on fruits, seeds, insects, and other invertebrates and often becomes more social outside the breeding season. It is also called the Mountain Robin or American Mountain Thrush.
value.classification: The Mountain Thrush belongs to the thrush family, Turdidae, in the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Turdus plebejus.
value.identification: This is a medium-sized, fairly plain thrush with olive-brown to brown upperparts and paler, warmer brown underparts. The breast and throat commonly show dusky or brown spotting, while the bill and legs are dark. Juveniles are generally duller and more heavily marked, with pale or buff edging on the wing feathers. It can resemble other brown mountain thrushes, but its combination of dark bare parts, overall brown plumage, and high-elevation habitat is useful for identification.
value.rangeHabitat: The Mountain Thrush has a disjunct range from southern Mexico through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and western Panama. In Costa Rica it occurs in the major mountain ranges, including the Cordilleras de Guanacaste, Central, and Talamanca. It inhabits montane evergreen forest, pine-oak forest, mature secondary woodland, and forest edges, especially where trees are rich in mosses and epiphytes. It may also use mossy trees in pastures, gardens, and open groves. Costa Rican records are mainly from about 900 to 3,500 meters, with breeding concentrated at higher elevations.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it moves downslope during the wettest part of the year, sometimes reaching about 900 meters, and commonly returns to higher elevations in January and February.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding is reported mainly from March through June. The nest is a broad, bulky cup made largely of green moss, with dry bamboo leaves and fine rootlets in the structure or lining. It is usually concealed among epiphytes on a tree, often about 3 to 12 meters above the ground, near forest edges or in the canopy. A typical clutch contains two or three blue-green eggs. Adults usually breed singly or in pairs.
value.dietFeeding: The Mountain Thrush eats a mixed diet of fruits, berries, seeds, insects, and other small invertebrates. It forages from the ground through the middle levels of vegetation and sometimes in the canopy, taking fallen or plant-produced food as well as animal prey. During the breeding season it is more often seen alone or in pairs. Outside that period, fruiting trees and open woodland may attract small groups.
value.behavior: This thrush is usually active within forest interiors, edges, and nearby open vegetation. It may forage quietly among mossy branches, epiphytes, and leaf litter, and it forms small flocks outside the breeding season. In Costa Rica, flocking and downslope movement are especially associated with the peak of the rainy season. Its vocal behavior includes a varied, warbling song and sharp, high-pitched calls, although it is often detected visually in suitable mountain habitat.

conservation.populationTrend: The total population has not been reliably quantified and is considered to be decreasing, but the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
